content: Is there a way to specialize a later (named) argument without introducing a new goal? For instance, given h : ∀x y, P x y in my context, I'd like to specialize by h (y := 6) to leave behind h : ∀x, P x 6 in the context

This is something specialize likely ought to be able to support. It's interesting though since h (y := 6) creates a lambda expression, not an application. Maybe it's reasonable if it figures out what it's replacing by looking for fun ... => h ...?

At least for now either Aaron's replace or have h := h (y := 6) work (the latter if you don't mind it not clearing h)
lean4#13528 is merged :tada:

Something that is useful for some internal purposes is to be able to specify named arguments by position (namely in elaborating dot notation).

The first syntax that came to mind is h (2 := 6), which would let you do specialize h (2 := 6), and it would be useful for when the names are not actually accessible, or for example implications where you can't see the name at all.

I thought I'd use this thread to ask if anyone had any ideas for this syntax. My mini-RFC is this: you could write f (idx := val) or f (@idx := val) depending on if you want to count the explicit arguments or count all arguments. This syntax would be available for applications in general, not just specialize

For a comparison, Rocq has a specialize h with (2 := 6) syntax.
The @ variant seems kinder on the parser :P

It's kind keeping the parser's well-being in our thoughts :slight_smile: I've checked that the parser is happy with (idx := val). I believe there's no ambiguity with the rest of the language, and the parser needs only the same lookahead as for named arguments.
(5 := 2 + 2) looks like somewhat cursed syntax to me; perhaps ([5] := 2 + 2) to invoke the idea of GetElem?
(though of course l[i] := 2 + 2 isn't currently legal anyway...)

The syntax { xs with [5] := 2+2 } exists

variable (xs : Array Nat)
#check { xs with [5] := 2 + 2}

but that's for array updates. This is meant to be used for { s with s.xs[5] := 2 + 2 }, where s is a structure, but it works on its own with just an array.

I gotta say as someone who's recently been fixing Rocq proofs this is one of my less-liked features lol
If you're iterating on definitions in a proof and you add an additional argument somewhere all of a sudden the numbers start shifting out from under you
However I do enjoy the convenience of things like replace a with b at 2, as cursed as that syntax looks
